note.explanation: The gradient of a distance-time graph tells you the average speed during a time interval. Find it by dividing the change in distance by the change in time.
examples: If distance changes by 12 m in 3 s, gradient = 12/3 = 4 m s⁻¹.
A horizontal distance-time line has gradient 0, so the body is at rest.
note.simple: Gradient tells you how much distance changes for each unit of time.
note.checkQuestion: A body covers 15 m in 3 s. What is the gradient of its distance-time graph?
note.title: Gradient of a Distance-Time Graph
steps: Find the change in distance: S₂ − S₁.
Find the change in time: t₂ − t₁.
Divide the change in distance by the change in time.
Write the result with suitable units.
note.answer: The gradient of a distance-time graph is equal to the average speed of the body.

mcqs.stem: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
rationales: Correct: gradient is change in distance divided by change in time, which is average speed.
Incorrect: distance is the vertical change, not the gradient itself.
Incorrect: acceleration is represented by the gradient of a speed-time graph.
Incorrect: time is the horizontal change, not the gradient itself.

mcqs.stem: Which expression gives the gradient between two points on a distance-time graph?
rationales: Correct: gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time.
Incorrect: this reverses the distance and time changes.
Incorrect: this gives only the change in distance.
Incorrect: this gives only the change in time.

mcqs.stem: What is the SI unit of the gradient of a distance-time graph when distance is measured in metres and time in seconds?
rationales: Correct: metres divided by seconds gives m s⁻¹.
Incorrect: m s is the product of the units, not distance divided by time.
Incorrect: s m⁻¹ is the reciprocal unit.
Incorrect: m² is an area unit.

mcqs.stem: What is the gradient of a horizontal line on a distance-time graph?
rationales: Correct: the distance does not change, so change in distance and gradient are zero.
Incorrect: a positive gradient would mean distance is increasing with time.
Incorrect: a negative gradient would mean the plotted distance is decreasing with time.
Incorrect: a horizontal line has a measurable gradient of zero.

options: The steeper line has the greater average speed
The less steep line has the greater average speed
Both lines must have equal average speed
Neither line gives information about average speed
mcqs.stem: Two straight rising lines are drawn on the same distance-time graph. What does a steeper line indicate?
rationales: Correct: a steeper distance-time line has a greater gradient and therefore greater average speed.
Incorrect: a less steep line has a smaller gradient.
Incorrect: the lines can have different gradients and speeds.
Incorrect: the gradients show the average speeds.

options: The object moves back toward its starting position
The object moves forward at constant speed
mcqs.stem: On a distance-time graph, what does a straight line with a negative gradient indicate?
rationales: Correct: the plotted distance decreases as time increases, indicating motion back toward the starting point.
Incorrect: a body at rest is represented by a horizontal line with zero gradient.
Incorrect: forward motion with increasing distance has a positive gradient.
Incorrect: a straight line indicates constant gradient, not constant acceleration.

written.text:
The figure given below shows the distance - time graph for the travel of a cyclist. Find the velocities for the segments a, b and c.

[FIGURE: Distance - time graph with vertical axis labelled “Distance → S (km)” and horizontal axis labelled “Time → t (min)”. The vertical scale is 0 to 2.0 in increments of 0.2; the horizontal scale is 0 to 20 in increments of 2. Segment a rises from (0, 0) to (6, 2.0), segment b is horizontal from (6, 2.0) to (10, 2.0), and segment c falls from (10, 2.0) to (20, 0).]
written.finalAnswer: a = 20 km h⁻¹; b = 0 km h⁻¹; c = −12 km h⁻¹

rubric.why: The gradient must be calculated from the change in distance divided by the change in time.
The cyclist's plotted distance does not change on segment b.
rubric.how: Show that the distance change over the 4-minute interval is zero.

rubric.why: The falling line has a negative gradient because the plotted distance decreases as time passes.
The final velocities must have the correct values, units, and sign for the direction shown by each segment.
rubric.how: Convert the gradients from km/min to km/h and keep the negative sign for segment c.

modelAnswer: For segment a: (2.0 − 0)/(6 − 0) = 1/3 km min⁻¹ = 20 km h⁻¹
For segment b: (2.0 − 2.0)/(10 − 6) = 0 km min⁻¹ = 0 km h⁻¹
For segment c: (0 − 2.0)/(20 − 10) = −0.2 km min⁻¹ = −12 km h⁻¹
Therefore, a = 20 km h⁻¹; b = 0 km h⁻¹; c = −12 km h⁻¹.

examTips: A board question may ask you to state what the gradient of a distance-time graph represents; write that it is the average speed.
For a graph calculation, select two points on the segment and show (S₂ − S₁)/(t₂ − t₁). Marks are commonly awarded for the correct changes, division, and final answer with units.
A horizontal segment has zero gradient. A falling segment has a negative gradient, so keep its sign when the question asks for velocity.

explain.title: What is gradient?
explain.body: The gradient is the measure of slope of a line. On a distance-time graph, it tells us how quickly distance changes as time passes.

explain.title: How to find the gradient
explain.body: Choose two points on the graph. The distance change is S₂ − S₁, and the time change is t₂ − t₁. Divide the distance change by the time change: gradient = (S₂ − S₁)/(t₂ − t₁).

explain.title: What the gradient means
explain.body: The book shows that S/t = v_av, the average speed during the time interval t. Therefore, the gradient of a distance-time graph is equal to the average speed of the body.

explain.title: Reading the shape
explain.body: A steeper rising line means a greater average speed. A horizontal segment has zero gradient. If the plotted distance falls as time increases, the gradient is negative.

mistakes: Dividing the change in time by the change in distance instead of distance by time.
Using only one point instead of finding changes between two points.
Forgetting the units, such as m s⁻¹ or km h⁻¹.
Dropping the negative sign for a segment where the plotted distance decreases.
Calling the gradient distance itself instead of average speed.
